meta.ogDescription: No source exists in Gandhi’s works. QI traces earlier variants (1914, 1944) and shows how biographer Louis Fischer’s phrasing seeded the false credit.

answer.label: Not Mahatma Gandhi — an unsourced modern epigram
answer.authorDates: 1869–1948 · Indian independence leader & apostle of nonviolence
answer.sourceLine: Widely pinned on Gandhi, but the exact wording is found in none of his writings or speeches. The Gandhi Institute for Nonviolence confirms “no example of its use by the Indian leader has ever been discovered.” The epigram is a twist on the Biblical eye for an eye (Exodus 21:24) that took shape gradually — earlier variants appear in 1914 and 1944, and biographer Louis Fischer used similar phrasing to describe Gandhi’s philosophy without ever quoting him.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Not found in any Gandhi writing, speech, or letter
1914 — George Perry Graham, Canadian House of Commons
Louis Fischer, characterizing Gandhi (1947 & 1950) — not a quotation of him

source.excerpt: An eye for an eye will make the whole world blind.
trail: The Gandhi Institute for Nonviolence reports the Gandhi family believes it authentic, yet “no example of its use by the Indian leader has ever been discovered.”

The earliest matching thought located by Quote Investigator is a 1914 remark by Canadian politician George Perry Graham that going back to “an eye for an eye” would leave the House “blind and toothless.”
Biographer Louis Fischer wrote of Gandhi’s creed as an “eye for an eye… which, in the end, would make everybody blind” (1947 & 1950) — but did not put the words in Gandhi’s mouth.
The clipped modern form also surfaces in Fiddler on the Roof, whose 1970s script has “the whole world will be blind and toothless.”
source.excerptNote: A crisp modern epigram built on the Biblical “eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Exodus 21:24). No version in Gandhi’s hand or voice has ever been located.
source.rightsNote: The exact epigram has no single identifiable author — it is an anonymous, gradually-evolved paraphrase of a Biblical injunction, first appearing in scattered variant forms in the early-to-mid 20th century. With no fixed source work or first-publication date to anchor it, no copyright status can be responsibly asserted.

author.name: Mahatma Gandhi
author.heading: About Mahatma Gandhi
author.metaLine: 1869–1948 · Indian independence leader & apostle of nonviolence
author.bio: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948) led India’s independence movement through satyagraha — nonviolent civil resistance — and became a global symbol of peaceful protest. His Collected Works run to roughly 100 volumes, yet this particular epigram appears in none of them. Its spirit is genuinely Gandhian; its crisp wording is a later invention that borrowed his name.

misattribution.heading: How Gandhi got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most-shared “Gandhi” lines — and one he is not documented as ever saying or writing.

items.why: Searches of Gandhi’s own writings and speeches turn up nothing; the Gandhi Institute for Nonviolence states “no example of its use by the Indian leader has ever been discovered.”

Fischer described Gandhi’s philosophy as an “eye for an eye… which, in the end, would make everybody blind” in 1947 and 1950 — without attributing the words to Gandhi. Readers appear to have mistaken his characterization for a quotation.

The blindness twist on Exodus 21:24 appears independently in 1914 (Canadian politician George Perry Graham) and 1944 (Henry Powell Spring), per Quote Investigator — showing the idea circulated without Gandhi’s name.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought fits Gandhi’s creed of nonviolence, but the polished epigram is an unsourced modern saying — no evidence ties it to his own words.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The line is repeated as Gandhi’s moral verdict on retaliation — from op-eds to protest signs to Fiddler on the Roof. Its staying power comes precisely from sounding like something he would have said, which is exactly how feel-good epigrams attach themselves to famous nonviolent icons.

The honest position is not that Gandhi rejected the sentiment — his whole philosophy of ahimsa embraced it — but that this specific sentence is a later crystallization by other hands, and crediting him by name overstates what the record supports.
context.pull: The spirit is Gandhian. The sentence is not his.
